algorithm: Thread-per-client TCP relay with line-based broadcast

classes.desc: Tiny TCP chat relay bound to 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port, one thread per client.
classes.name: ChatServer

classes.desc: Blocking-line chat client with a background reader thread and a received-message inbox.
classes.name: ChatClient

complexity: O(n) broadcast per message over n clients
data_flow_ascii:
client -> TCP line -> server reader thread -> broadcast()
broadcast() -> all other clients' sockets -> client inbox
self-test compares each inbox against the expected transcript
description_sentence: A loopback-only TCP chat server that relays messages between clients, with a default self-test that verifies delivery end to end.
failure_note: Dead clients are removed from the broadcast list on read errors; shutdown() closes every socket and joins the accept thread.

label: chat server
output_shape: Prints each client's received transcript plus a PASS/FAIL relay check; --serve prints the bound address and runs until Ctrl-C.
pitch_sentence: I built a {topic} that relays messages between local clients in real time, with a self-test proving every message arrives.

qa.a: Loopback-only binding keeps the demo safe: no traffic ever leaves the machine and no firewall port is opened.
qa.q: Why does the server bind only 127.0.0.1?

qa.a: Two scripted clients exchange messages; the test compares each client's inbox against the exact expected transcript and prints PASS or FAIL.
qa.q: How does the default run verify the relay?

qa.a: Newline-delimited lines; each side buffers bytes and splits on newlines so partial TCP reads are reassembled correctly.

resume_bullet_template: Built a {topic} in Python with sockets and threads, including a scripted two-client self-test that verifies message relay.
run_notes: --serve runs the server persistently; --messages sets the per-client message count for the self-test.
scaling_note: Thread-per-client suits a demo; hundreds of clients would want selectors or asyncio instead of one thread each.
storage_note: In-memory only: messages live in client inboxes during the run and are discarded on shutdown.
tech_stack: stdlib: argparse, random, socket, threading, time
tradeoff_note: Blocking sockets with threads are simple and readable, at the cost of per-client thread overhead versus an event loop.
